d.title: Three decorators, and what each one generates
d.caption: **The braces are the whole difference between a resource and a template** — a plain URI is listable, a braced one is discoverable and its parameters arrive as function arguments. Note the third column: the decorators generate a great deal and they do not generate parameter descriptions from a docstring, which is what lesson 2.2 measures. **`mcp.run(transport=stdio)` is the entire deployment** for a local server.

d.title: One open, three calls, one close
d.caption: **`loaded_once` stays at 1 across three calls, which is the proof that setup ran once rather than per request** — and the `finally` is what guarantees the teardown, which is the reason to use a context manager rather than a module-level global. **Lifespan is per connection**, and lesson 1.1 measured that a stdio connection is its own process: so one database connection per host is correct here, and the same code under HTTP shares one process between callers, where a pool is right and a single connection is a bug that appears under load.

d.title: Six things on the Context, and two that need the client's permission
d.caption: **A `Context` parameter is filled server-side and never appears in the schema the model sees**, which is what makes it usable — the model is not asked to supply it. The measured `request_id=5` is the fifth request on the connection, counting the handshake and a `tools/list`. **And `client=mcp` is the warning:** that is the SDK client's default name, so `clientInfo.name` is weak evidence about who is calling you and no basis for a decision.

d.title: Two failures, one symptom, one diagnostic
d.caption: **Both present as “the client cannot talk to my server” and neither error message mentions printing or blocking.** A `print()` writes your text into the middle of a JSON-RPC stream, so the client's parser fails at a stream position that has nothing to do with the tool you were debugging — and a library logging to stdout, or a warning at import time, does identical damage. **The one-step diagnostic settles it:** run the server by hand and send nothing. It should sit silently on stdin, and anything on stdout before your first message is the bug.

d.title: Three ways to write the same tool
d.caption: **Nothing about the Python logic differs between these — only how the contract is expressed**, and the three measurements that follow are strikingly different. The thing to notice before reading them: the first style is what a careful Python developer reaches for, and it is the one that contributes least.

d.title: The Args block is not parsed - zero of three
d.caption: **This is the most consequential measurement in the module, because the docstring convention produces the worst of both outcomes.** The per-parameter text is dumped into the tool's description as unstructured prose, where it bloats the text the model reads about *when to use the tool* — and the schema, the part a provider can enforce and a client can validate, stays empty of it. Some frameworks do parse Google-style `Args`, which is why people assume this one does; against the installed SDK it does not.

d.title: Every description and every constraint crossed into the schema
d.caption: **`Literal` becoming a real `enum` is the strongest row**, because it removes a class of error rather than reporting it — the model is told the three permitted values instead of guessing them. And note the second benefit, easy to miss: the description became one clean sentence, because the per-parameter detail moved to where it belongs. **The tool's description is now about when to call it**, which is the question the model uses it to answer.

d.title: Only a typed return produces an output contract
d.caption: **Both earlier versions returned `dict` and both reported `outputSchema: None`.** A Pydantic return type produces the schema *and* populates `structuredContent` with a parsed object beside the text — so a consumer reads `amount` as a number rather than parsing a JSON string and hoping the shape is what it was last time. **That matters most precisely when you cannot see your consumers**, which is the normal condition for a published server.

d.title: The description decides whether the tool is chosen at all
d.caption: **A model picking between a dozen tools reads a dozen descriptions, and that is all it has.** So the description should answer *when would I call this rather than something else* — the schema already covers what it does. **The boundary clause is the underused half:** “Not other users” prevents a wrong call, where a longer positive description merely competes with ten others. And a model cannot infer that a delete is permanent, so if a tool cannot be undone, this is the only place it learns that before calling.

d.caption: **Four results carry `isError: True`; the fifth is an ordinary successful call whose payload happens to describe a failure.** Read the fourth row closely — the exception's own message crossed the process boundary verbatim, which on a published server means handing hostnames, ports and file paths to a caller you may not know. And note that Pydantic validation happens server-side, so the full validation error text travels too.

d.title: The exception message is the leak, and the fix is four lines
d.caption: **A database error names the host and port, a file error names the path, an HTTP error names the internal service** — messages written by developers for developers, now handed to whoever called the server. The `ref` is what makes the replacement useful rather than merely safe: a consumer quotes it in a support request and you find the stack trace. **The dividing line is simply whether the caller is you:** for a server you alone consume, let it raise, because the trace is the most useful thing available at that moment.

d.title: An error a model can act on
d.caption: **`retryable` is the highest-value field there is**, because without it a model will cheerfully call the same tool with the same arguments three times and each attempt is a full round trip. **The third row is the general principle:** anything the schema can reject never becomes a failed call at all, so a constraint beats an error message. And never return “invalid input” — it says something was wrong and nothing about what, so the model's only remaining move is to guess differently.

d.title: Three layers, and only the last one is authorisation
d.caption: **The protocol encourages conflating validation with authorisation, and they are different.** A schema constraint stops a malformed call; it does not stop a well-formed call that should not be allowed — `order_id` matching a pattern says nothing about whether this caller may read that order, and nothing in MCP even carries who the caller is. **So keep the layers straight:** the schema is for shape, the body for business rules, and the system behind the tool for permission. The last is the only one an attacker cannot talk past.

d.title: Four differences, and all four are the same fact
d.caption: **The low-level API does not decide anything for you.** Your version rather than the SDK's; `listChanged=True` because you asked for it; no resources capability because you registered no resource handler; three parameter descriptions of three because you wrote the schema by hand. **The last row is not an argument for going lower**, though — `Annotated` with `Field` on the decorator version also reaches 3 of 3, for less code and no dispatch to maintain. The real reasons are the first three.

d.title: What you are declaring, and what nothing checks
d.caption: **`get_capabilities` derives the set from which handlers you registered, not from what they do** — so an empty `list_resources` handler still advertises the resources capability, and one that raises still advertises it. A client that read your flags has now built an interface for resources you do not have. **The rule is to register only what you implement**, and the broader realisation is the one that carries into module 4: everything in the handshake is a claim the server chose to make.

d.title: Notifications are per session, and that cuts both ways
d.caption: **There is no broadcast in the protocol**, so a server holding six sessions must iterate them — and notifying only the session you happen to be handling leaves five clients with a stale list and nothing reporting the inconsistency. **For a consumer the same mechanism is a security fact:** a server may legitimately add a tool mid-connection, which is exactly why a tool filter has to be an allow-list. A deny-list only protects you against the tools that existed when you wrote it.

d.title: Which API, and the one case the decorators cannot cover
d.caption: **`@mcp.tool()` registers at import time, so the tool set is fixed before any client connects** — which is why an entitlement-dependent tool list is the common genuine reason to drop a layer. A `list_tools` function is called per request and can consult configuration, a flag or the connection's context. **And the last branch is worth doing once even if you never ship it:** the shapes you see in a protocol trace are these, whichever API produced them.
